questions.stem: Which radiation is a helium nucleus?
questions.explanation: An alpha particle is ${}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}$: two protons and two neutrons, the nucleus of a helium-4 atom. Beta is an electron from the nucleus; gamma is a photon. X-rays are also photons, produced electronically in a tube rather than by nuclear decay.

distractorRationale.b: A beta particle is a fast electron, ${}^{0}_{-1}e$, not a helium nucleus
distractorRationale.c: Gamma is electromagnetic radiation, with no mass and no charge
distractorRationale.d: Hospital X-rays are photons like gamma, but they are made by decelerating electrons, not by a decaying nucleus

questions.stem: Which listed radiation has the greatest penetrating power?
questions.explanation: Gamma photons have no charge and interact only occasionally, so they can cross metres of air and need thick lead or concrete to be reduced substantially. Alpha is stopped by paper or a few centimetres of air; beta by a few millimetres of aluminium. Penetrating power and ionising power are opposites.

distractorRationale.a: Alpha is the most ionising and therefore the least penetrating — it spends its energy in a short track
distractorRationale.b: Beta is intermediate; aluminium stops it, whereas gamma still gets through
distractorRationale.d: A slow proton is a charged massive particle and ionises densely, so it does not penetrate far

questions.stem: In the decay ${}^{234}_{90}\mathrm{Th} \rightarrow {}^{A}_{Z}\mathrm{Pa} + {}^{0}_{-1}e$, the values of $A$ and $Z$ are
questions.explanation: Beta-minus emission: a neutron becomes a proton, so $A$ is unchanged (234) and $Z$ increases by 1 (90 + 1 = 91). Checking the beta particle: $A$: $234 = 234 + 0$; $Z$: $90 = 91 + (-1)$. Option a is what alpha decay of this parent would give.

distractorRationale.a: Those numbers are for α decay (A − 4, Z − 2), not β decay
distractorRationale.c: This lowers Z, which would be a positron (β⁺) emission, not β⁻
distractorRationale.d: Those are the numbers of uranium-238, a typical parent of thorium, not the daughter of this decay

questions.stem: When ${}^{226}_{88}\mathrm{Ra}$ emits an alpha particle, the nuclide formed is
questions.explanation: Alpha is ${}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}$, so $A$ falls by 4 ($226 - 4 = 222$) and $Z$ falls by 2 ($88 - 2 = 86$). $Z = 86$ is radon. The nuclear equation is ${}^{226}_{88}\mathrm{Ra} \rightarrow {}^{222}_{86}\mathrm{Rn} + {}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}$.

distractorRationale.a: Z increased by 1, which is β⁻ decay, and A is unchanged
distractorRationale.c: Z is correct for radon but A was not reduced by 4
distractorRationale.d: A is correct but Z was left as radium; the element must change when Z changes

questions.stem: A radioactive sample of half-life 8.0 days has an initial mass of 80 g. Calculate the mass of that nuclide remaining after 24 days. Give your answer in grams.
questions.explanation: Number of half-lives $n = 24 / 8.0 = 3$. Remaining mass $= 80 \times (1/2)^{3} = 80 / 8 = 10\ \text{g}$. Dividing 80 by 24 would give about 3.3 g, which treats half-life as if the sample vanished linearly with time.

questions.stem: The most appropriate precaution when handling a sealed gamma source in a school laboratory is to

options.text: hold it in the palm of the hand so that it cannot be dropped
use long tongs, keep exposure time short, and store it in a lead castle
wrap it in a single sheet of paper, which stops all ionising radiation
heat it first so that the activity falls

questions.explanation: Dose is reduced by time, distance and shielding. Tongs increase distance; a short experiment reduces time; lead absorbs a useful fraction of gamma. Paper stops alpha, not gamma. Heating does not change a nuclear half-life.

distractorRationale.a: The hand is the worst place: high dose, no distance, no shielding, and gamma goes through tissue
distractorRationale.c: Paper stops alpha particles; gamma needs dense, thick shielding such as lead
distractorRationale.d: Radioactive decay is independent of temperature; heating the source does not make it safer

questions.stem: A beam containing α, β and γ radiation enters a uniform magnetic field directed into the page. Which statement is correct?

options.text: All three radiations go straight on, because they are uncharged
Gamma is undeflected; alpha and beta are deflected in opposite directions, beta more sharply
Alpha and gamma are undeflected; only beta bends
All three are deflected the same way, because they come from the same nucleus

questions.explanation: A magnetic field deflects moving charges. Gamma has no charge, so it is undeflected. Alpha is positive and relatively massive, so it bends one way on a gentle arc. Beta is negative and much lighter, so it bends the opposite way on a tighter arc. This is the classic deflection diagram in WAEC papers.

distractorRationale.a: Only gamma is uncharged; alpha and beta are charged particles
distractorRationale.c: Alpha has charge +2e, so it is deflected, though less than beta
distractorRationale.d: Opposite charges deflect opposite ways; origin in the same nucleus does not give them the same charge

questions.stem: The activity of a source is 800 Bq. Its half-life is 2.0 h. Calculate the activity after 6.0 h. Give your answer in becquerels.
questions.explanation: Three half-lives elapse ($6.0 / 2.0 = 3$), so the activity is halved three times: $800 \rightarrow 400 \rightarrow 200 \rightarrow 100\ \text{Bq}$. Equivalently $A = 800 \times (1/2)^{3} = 100\ \text{Bq}$. Subtracting 6 from 800 as if decay were linear would give 794 Bq, which is not how half-life works.
